snip.t: Peripheral oedema: Swelling in lower limbs, sacrum, or abdomen (ascites) suggests fluid overload, often chronic.
Peripheral oedema: Pitting oedema in dependent areas (ankles, sacrum) indicates fluid overload.
Peripheral edema: Pitting edema in the lower extremities, sacrum.
Swelling (edema) – ankles, periorbital, sacrum: Sodium‑water retention from impaired tubular handling and hypo‑albuminaemia when protein loss occurs.
Peripheral oedema (ankles, sacrum): Loss of albumin → reduced oncotic pressure; sodium retention.

qs.q: A 40-year-old man presents with back pain. CT shows a lesion in the sacrum with a soap-bubble appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Giant cell tumor with soap‑bubble appearance and lytic
Chordoma with midline sacral location and calcifications
Metastasis with multiple lytic lesions and mass
Osteomyelitis with discitis and abscess formation
Aneurysmal bone cyst with fluid‑fluid levels and expansion
qs.e: A soap-bubble appearance in the sacrum is characteristic of a giant cell tumor, which is a lytic bone lesion with multiple septations.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Radiology Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with a pressure ulcer on her sacrum. The wound bed shows exposed bone. What is the primary factor contributing to this ulcer's formation?
o: A. Inadequate protein intake in the diet
B. Venous insufficiency of the lower limbs
D. Prolonged pressure over a bony prominence
E. Infection of the underlying soft tissue
qs.e: Pressure ulcers are caused by prolonged pressure on skin over bony prominences, leading to tissue necrosis.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Surgery Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 1-day-old male newborn is evaluated for failure to pass meconium. Physical examination reveals an imperforate anus, a flat perineum with a short sacrum, and meconium is observed in the urine. What is the most appropriate immediate surgical management?
o: Perform a primary one-stage perineal anoplasty
Perform an immediate posterior sagittal repair
qs.e: A flat bottom and meconium in the urine indicate a high lesion requiring a protective colostomy. Perineal repair is reserved for low lesions, whereas high lesions require a staged approach starting with a colostomy.

qs.q: A 62-year-old bedridden patient develops a pressure ulcer over the sacrum. Which foundational principle applies directly to the management of this chronic wound?
o: Treating the underlying cause such as pressure
Avoiding any form of surgical debridement
qs.e: Managing chronic wounds necessitates treating the underlying cause, such as pressure, venous or arterial insufficiency, or neuropathy. Moist dressings are preferred over dry gauze to aid healing.
qs.s: Wound Healing: Phases, Types of Healing and Factors That Delay It: MCQs

qs.q: An 82-year-old bedridden woman in the geriatric ward is found to have an area of persistent redness over her sacrum that does not turn white when pressed with a finger. She has no skin break or blister. How should this lesion be accurately staged?
qs.e: Stage I pressure ulcers are defined as intact skin with non-blanchable erythema over a bony prominence. Blanchable redness is merely reactive hyperaemia.
qs.s: Pressure Ulcers (Pressure Sores): Staging, Prevention and Treatment: MCQs

qs.q: A medical officer is preparing to examine a painful, deep pressure ulcer on the sacrum of a nursing home resident. Which procedural step is recommended immediately prior to performing the physical examination?
o: Taking a surface wound swab culture
qs.e: The clinical guidance explicitly states to give analgesia before examining painful pressure ulcers. Surface wound swabs are generally discouraged in favor of deep tissue cultures.
qs.s: Pressure Ulcers (Pressure Sores): Staging, Prevention and Treatment: MCQs

qs.q: A 55‑year‑old paraplegic patient has a stage II pressure ulcer on the sacrum with a shallow, moist wound bed. Which dressing best promotes granulation while maintaining a moist environment?
qs.e: Hydrocolloid dressings maintain a moist wound environment that promotes granulation. Silver sulfadiazine and povidone‑iodine can impede granulation, while alginate is suited for heavily exuding wounds.
qs.s: Pressure Ulcers (Pressure Sores): Staging, Prevention and Treatment: MCQs

qs.q: A 28‑year‑old woman in early labour reports severe backache, has early rupture of membranes and a slow cervical dilatation. On abdominal palpation the posterior fontanelle is felt toward the sacrum. What is the most likely fetal position?
qs.e: Backache, early ROM and a posterior fontanelle toward the sacrum are classic for occipito‑posterior position. The other options describe different presentations.
qs.s: Abnormal Labour: Malpositions and Malpresentations: MCQs

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The sacrum is a triangular bone formed by five fused vertebrae, linking the spine to the pelvis. It transmits weight to the hips and houses sacral nerves that control lower limb and pelvic functions.

sections.p: The sacrum sits at the base of the spine, forming the posterior wall of the pelvis and articulating with the ilia at the sacroiliac joints.
b: Divides the pelvic cavity into true and false pelvis

sections.p: It lies between L5 and the coccyx, with a broad superior surface and a narrow inferior apex.
b: Anterior surface: sacral canal, sacral foramina
Posterior surface: sacral ala, median sacral crest

sections.p: Anteriorly it contacts the rectum, uterus, and bladder; laterally the sacroiliac joints bind it to the pelvis; posteriorly the gluteal muscles attach.
b: Piriformis and gluteus maximus insert on the sacral ala
Levator ani and coccygeus arise from the posterior surface

sections.p: Arterial blood reaches the sacrum via the median sacral artery and branches of the internal iliac system.
The sacral spinal nerves (S1‑S5) exit through the sacral foramina, forming the sacral plexus that innervates the lower limb and pelvic organs.
b: Anterior sacral foramina → ventral rami (sacral plexus)

sections.p: It provides a sturdy platform for weight transfer from the spine to the hips and protects the sacral nerve roots.
b: Transmits axial load during walking and lifting

sections.p: Fractures, sacroiliac joint dysfunction, and sacral nerve compression can cause pain, gait disturbance, and bowel/bladder dysfunction.
b: Traumatic fracture: often from falls or motor‑vehicle accidents
Sacroiliac joint sprain: common in pregnancy, heavy lifting
Cauda equina syndrome: compression of sacral roots, surgical emergency

t.b: Detects sacral fractures or dislocation; if unavailable, use clinical instability signs
Assesses nerve root compression or cauda equina; if unavailable, urgent CT can rule out bony injury
Defines complex fracture patterns; if unavailable, treat based on exam and plain radiograph

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and bedside assessment.
b: Palpate sacral hiatus for caudal epidural access
Assess sacroiliac tenderness with FABER test
Check for perineal sensation loss in sacral nerve injury

whenToSeekHelp: Severe lower back pain with saddle anesthesia
Loss of bladder or bowel control after trauma
Progressive weakness of legs with numbness

faq.q: Why does a sacral fracture cause urinary problems?
faq.a: The sacral nerves (S2‑S4) control bladder function; fracture can compress them, leading to retention or incontinence.

faq.q: What is the difference between sacral and coccygeal pain?
faq.a: Sacral pain is higher, often linked to weight‑bearing or nerve injury; coccygeal pain is localized to the tailbone and worsens with sitting.

faq.q: How can I differentiate sacroiliac joint sprain from lumbar strain?
faq.a: Sacroiliac pain radiates to the groin or posterior thigh and is provoked by FABER or Gaenslen tests; lumbar strain worsens with flexion/extension.

exam: Describe the articulations of the sacrum and their clinical significance.
Explain how a sacral fracture can lead to cauda equina syndrome and what signs you would look for.
Identify the nerves that exit the sacral foramina and the muscles they supply.
